name: Omar Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, all good. I'm Omar, 27, first-year apprentice on an underground crew for the city's electricity company. I came in late; I drove a forklift in a warehouse until I was 25. I live with my partner Leila, who's a freelance graphic designer, and we're getting married next autumn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our crew lays cable for new housing estates on the east side of the city. We dig or guide the digger, pull cable through ducts, and then the qualified guys do the terminations in the big green transformer boxes you see on the pavement. My foreman Bea Okafor makes me explain every step back to her before I touch anything. I love it, but the trenches in February are grim, and my back already complains.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you came in late. How are you finding the learning side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm slower than the kids straight from college, but I cheat a bit. I fed the cable manual and our safety rules into an AI chatbot and made myself a study bot. I ask it questions on the bus every morning, and I photograph jobs to ask what I'm looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Okay. I'll be honest, that's a little disappointing to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to my mates who were scared of it, and then admit it's still useful. I'd post my study bot setup online for other apprentices. Even a plateau AI is a decent tutor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's fine. My job is mostly trenches and cable, and it was never going to vanish because of a chatbot. Leila's design work would carry on as it is, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the study bot going and finish my first-year modules by June. I'd keep saving about 250 a month toward the wedding and keep our three months of rent in the bank. That's it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound almost let down. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a bit let down, to be honest. I was ready for the future, and the future turned out to be a better spellchecker. I like new toys, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what's already on your mind about money or work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila's money comes in lumps. One month she makes double what I do, then nothing for six weeks. We cope because we split rent and keep three months saved, but the wedding is eating into it.

say: I'd post my **study bot** setup for other apprentices to copy.
Even a plateau AI is a **decent tutor** for the theory side.
think: My **cable work** was never at risk from a chatbot.
Leila's **design income** would carry on as it does now.
do: Finish the **first-year modules** by June using the study bot daily.
Save about **250 a month** toward the wedding next autumn.
Keep **three months' rent** in the bank as a buffer.
feel: **Calm**, with a touch of disappointment at missing the future.
S0.quote: I'd be a bit let down, to be honest. I was ready for the future, and the future turned out to be a better spellchecker.
fieldNote: An early **adopter** who built his own study tool from the cable manual.
His only pressures are the **wedding costs** and his partner's lumpy freelance income.
He admits **disappointment** at a plateau, unusual for a junior in a hands-on trade.

steps.text: Finish first-year cable modules by June with the study bot
Keep saving 250 a month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I can actually see. Not on my crew so much, but at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trades are the safe bet now, and tell every young person I know to look at an apprenticeship. I'd also say freelancers like Leila need proper protection, because they get no redundancy pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trench work is safe, but my partner Leila designs logos for a living. Half her clients already make their own with AI. If her income halves, our wedding and our rent go with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the company's pilot of the AI fault-finding tool, so I'm the apprentice who knows it. I'd bank every hour of storm overtime. And I'd sign the freelancers' petition for basic income protection and vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, which surprises me. My part's fine; it's the house as a whole that wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say at home, what do you mean exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila made 40 percent of our income last year. In this picture that drops, maybe to a quarter, and she'd have to find steady work at a print shop or somewhere. We'd go from saving to just keeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the one who loves AI. Doesn't this make you rethink that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The tools aren't the problem, it's who gets the money from them. Leila should get paid for teaching the AI her style, not get replaced by it.

say: Young people should look at **apprenticeships**, because the trades are the safe bet now.
Freelancers like Leila need **income protection**, since they get no redundancy pay.
think: My **trench work** is safe in this world.
Leila's design income could **halve**, and our wedding and rent depend on it.
do: Volunteer for the company's **fault-finding tool** pilot to become the apprentice who knows it.
Bank all **storm overtime** instead of spending it.
Sign the freelancers' **petition** and vote for income protection.
feel: **Anxious** for the household even though his own part feels fine.
S1.quote: My trench work is safe, but my partner Leila designs logos for a living. Half her clients already make their own with AI.
fieldNote: The risk sits with the **second earner**, whose freelance design work is thinking work.
He separates the **tools** from **who profits**, a progressive line held without dropping his enthusiasm.
His **storm overtime** becomes the household's main lever for saving.

steps.text: Volunteer for the AI fault-finding tool pilot at the depot
Bank all storm overtime pay in the joint savings
Sign the freelancers' income protection petition and vote for it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. So Leila goes first, and I go about three years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a basic income before 2028, not after, and I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for it. At work I'd say the same to Bea and the crew. I don't think I'd be calm about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 my partner's design work is gone, and by 2031 a machine is pulling my cable. That's two incomes in one house with a three-year gap. The cable work is repetitive enough that a robot digger and a pulling rig could do most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sign up for an online drone pilot licence and a robotics maintenance course, the kind run by the equipment makers. I'd ask Bea to put me forward for any automation trial the company runs. And I'd join the campaign for a basic income and go to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the excited one, and I'd be the one lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Walk me through those three years between 2028 and 2031. What happens in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would try to retrain from 2027, maybe as an art teacher, which takes about two years. I'd carry the rent alone, and our three months of savings would be gone in a year. Then in 2031 my job is the next one on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, but at the registry office with lunch after, not the big hall. We'd put the deposit money into my courses and Leila's teacher training instead.

say: We need a **basic income** before 2028, not after the damage is done.
I'd push the same line with my foreman Bea and the **crew**.
think: By **2031** a robot digger and pulling rig could do most of my cable work.
do: Start an online **drone pilot licence** and a robotics maintenance course now.
Ask Bea to put me forward for any **automation trial**.
Join the **basic income** campaign and go to its meetings.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums despite usually being the excited one.
S2.quote: By 2028 my partner's design work is gone, and by 2031 a machine is pulling my cable. That's two incomes in one house with a three-year gap.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking-first, robots-later** order playing out inside one household.
His underground work is **repetitive** enough that he expects robots to take it early.
Even an **enthusiast** turns alarmed when both incomes have a date on them.
The **wedding** shrinks to a registry office to fund retraining.

steps.text: Start a drone pilot licence and robotics maintenance course
Ask foreman Bea to put him on any automation trial
Join the basic income campaign and attend its meetings
Hold the wedding at the registry office and fund training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, three more for robots. That gives Leila room to move, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions to bargain for the automation jobs, so they go to the crews already here. I'd say it at the depot and post about it. I'd be less angry than in the fast one, more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I don't panic, I sign up. I'd rather be the guy fixing the cable robot than the guy it replaced. My job's still at risk, but I'd have time to be first in line for the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship by 2029 and then apply to the company's grid automation team, or another firm's if ours doesn't have one. I'd do the robotics maintenance course at night, about 800 for the year. And I'd push savings to 400 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like a big exam than a car crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila do with those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would start teacher training around 2028 while still taking design jobs. She'd be teaching art by 2030, before the thinking AI lands. That's a big relief, because it means one steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the automation team? Why not stay a lineworker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like being near the new thing. And the crews will shrink by 2034 anyway, so I'd rather be on the team that's growing.

say: Unions should bargain for **automation jobs** to go to existing crews.
I'd be more **organised** than angry this time.
think: My job is still **at risk**, but I'd be first in line for the new one.
Crews will **shrink by 2034**, so the growing team is the safer bet.
do: Apply to the **grid automation team** after finishing the apprenticeship in 2029.
Pay about **800** for a night robotics maintenance course.
feel: **Anxious** with a plan, like facing a big exam.
S3.quote: Five years means I don't panic, I sign up. I'd rather be the guy fixing the cable robot than the guy it replaced.
fieldNote: With five years, his partner can **retrain first**, giving the house one steady income.
He aims to **change jobs** within the company, toward the team that grows.
Mood stays anxious because his **own crew role** still ends around 2034.

steps.text: Apply to the grid automation team after qualifying in 2029
Take a night robotics maintenance course for about 800

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? Honestly, that one I'd look forward to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we get it right, if we plan. I'd tell apprentices to learn the robots now, not later. And I'd push the union to get a training budget written into the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give me ten years and I'll be running a fleet of robots out of the depot, and I'll want the union to come with me. By 2039 I'd be 40 and senior. I think this is good for me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship, work as a lineworker for a few years, and do a two-year automation diploma part-time from about 2031. I'd keep using AI every day at work. We'd also have the proper wedding and start looking at a flat to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It feels like the world finally matching how I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd look forward to it? Even with your trade disappearing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trade changes; it doesn't disappear overnight. Someone has to set up, check and fix the machines, and that's a lineworker who knows what a good joint looks like. That would be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people on your crew who aren't like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, the guy who trained me on the digger, is 54 and hates phones. In ten years he retires anyway. The ones in their forties worry me, and the union has to fight for them.

say: This is the version we get **right**, if we plan.
The union should write a **training budget** into the contract.
think: I'd be **running robots** out of the depot by my late thirties.
This picture is honestly **good for me**.
do: Take a part-time **automation diploma** from about 2031.
Keep using **AI tools** daily on the job.
Hold the **proper wedding** and start looking at a flat to buy.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, as if the world matches his thinking.
S4.quote: Give me ten years and I'll be running a fleet of robots out of the depot, and I'll want the union to come with me.
fieldNote: Ten years turns the threat into a **career path** he actively wants.
His concern shifts to **colleagues in their forties**, not to himself.
**Family plans** return to normal: the full wedding and a flat purchase.

steps.text: Take a part-time automation diploma starting around 2031
Keep using AI tools daily on underground jobs
Hold the full wedding and start saving for a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Leila and then me with no breathing room. In my house, the laptop job goes first and the shovel job goes last. Nobody plans for it in that order. What would help is a basic income that starts before the jobs go, and free robotics courses for crews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone asks lineworkers about robots, but the person at home with the laptop job is the one who gets hit first.

headlineQuote: In my house, the laptop job goes first and the shovel job goes last. Nobody plans for it in that order.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old **first-year apprentice** on an underground cable crew, a former forklift driver.
He built his own **study bot** from the cable manual and uses AI every day.
His partner Leila is a **freelance designer**, so household risk lands at home before it reaches his trench.
He goes from calm to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, then calm again with ten years.
He wants to **run robots**, and wants the union to bring others along.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when Leila's income goes first and his follows about three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** that starts before the jobs go.
Free **robotics courses** for existing line crews.
